# Git Version Control Fundamentals

> **⚠️ DEMO MODE** — Generated with built-in sample content because no Gemini API key is configured.
> Add `GEMINI_API_KEY` to `.env` for AI-generated lessons.

## Learning Objective
Use core Git commands (init, add, commit, branch, merge) to track changes and manage branches in a local repository.

---

## ⏱️ Time Breakdown

| Section | Time |
|---|---|
| Introduction | 5 min |
| Core Content: What is Git? | 7 min |
| Core Content: Essential Commands | 10 min |
| Core Content: Branching & Merging | 10 min |
| Practical Application | 7 min |
| Knowledge Check | 4 min |
| Summary & Wrap-up | 2 min |
| **Total** | **45 min** |

---

## 1. Introduction (5 min)

Imagine writing a 50-page report and accidentally deleting half of it — with no Undo. Version control prevents exactly that. **Git** is the world's most widely used version control system, underpinning platforms like GitHub, GitLab, and Bitbucket.

**Opening question:** *Have you ever accidentally overwritten a file and wished you could go back?*

---

## 2. What is Git? (7 min)

Git is a **distributed version control system** (DVCS):
- Every developer has a **full copy** of the repository.
- Changes are tracked as **snapshots** (not diffs) over time.
- It works **offline** — you can commit, branch, and view history without internet.

**Key concepts:**

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| Repository (repo) | The folder tracked by Git + its entire history |
| Commit | A saved snapshot of the project at a point in time |
| Branch | An independent line of development |
| Merge | Combining changes from two branches |
| HEAD | Pointer to the currently checked-out commit/branch |

> 📖 **Source:** [Pro Git Book — Chapter 1](https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2/Getting-Started-What-is-Git%3F)

---

## 3. Essential Commands (10 min)

### Setting up
```bash
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"
```

### Starting a repository
```bash
git init my-project    # Create a new repo
cd my-project
```

### The staging area workflow
```
Working Directory → (git add) → Staging Area → (git commit) → Repository
```

```bash
git status             # See what's changed
git add README.md      # Stage a specific file
git add .              # Stage all changes
git commit -m "Add README"  # Save a snapshot
git log --oneline      # View commit history
```

> 📖 **Source:** [Git Documentation — git-scm.com](https://git-scm.com/docs)

### Checking and undoing
```bash
git diff               # See unstaged changes
git restore <file>     # Discard working-directory changes
git restore --staged <file>  # Unstage a file
```

---

## 4. Branching & Merging (10 min)

Branches let you develop features or fix bugs in isolation.

```bash
git branch             # List branches
git branch feature-x   # Create a new branch
git checkout feature-x # Switch to it
# (shortcut: git checkout -b feature-x)

# Make changes and commit on feature-x...
git add .
git commit -m "Add feature X"

# Merge back into main
git checkout main
git merge feature-x    # Fast-forward or creates a merge commit
```

**Visualising branches:**
```
main:      A---B---C
                    \
feature-x:           D---E
                          -> merge into main: A---B---C---M
```

**Merge conflicts** happen when the same lines were changed on both branches. Git marks conflicts like:
```
<<<<<<< HEAD
Your version
=======
Their version
>>>>>>> feature-x
```
Edit the file to resolve, then `git add` and `git commit`.

> 📖 **Source:** [Pro Git — Branching](https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2/Git-Branching-Branches-in-a-Nutshell)
> 🎥 **Git and GitHub for Beginners — freeCodeCamp:** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RGOj5yH7evk

---

## 5. Practical Application (7 min)

**Hands-on exercise:**
```bash
# 1. Create and initialise a repo
git init demo-repo && cd demo-repo

# 2. Create a file, stage, and commit
echo "# My Project" > README.md
git add README.md
git commit -m "Initial commit"

# 3. Create a branch and make changes
git checkout -b add-info
echo "More info here." >> README.md
git add README.md
git commit -m "Add more info"

# 4. Merge back to main
git checkout main
git merge add-info

# 5. View the full history
git log --oneline --graph --all
```

Expected output for step 5:
```
*   abc1234 (HEAD -> main) Merge branch 'add-info'
|\
| * def5678 (add-info) Add more info
|/
* ghi9012 Initial commit
```

*(Note: your commit hashes will differ from the examples above.)*

---

## 6. Knowledge Check (4 min)

**Question 1:** What command do you use to stage all changed files?

**Question 2:** What single command creates a new branch called `feature-name` AND switches to it?

**Question 3:** After merging `feature-x` into `main`, you see conflict markers. What are the three steps to resolve the conflict?

**Question 4:** What is the difference between `git restore <file>` and `git restore --staged <file>`?

---

### ✅ Answer Key

**Q1:** `git add .`

**Q2:** `git checkout -b feature-name`

**Q3:** (1) Edit the file to remove conflict markers and keep the correct content. (2) `git add <file>`. (3) `git commit` (Git auto-generates the merge commit message).

**Q4:** `git restore <file>` discards **working-directory** changes (un-edits the file). `git restore --staged <file>` moves a file from the staging area back to the working directory (un-stages it) without changing the file content.

---

## 7. Supplementary Resources

- 🎥 **Git and GitHub for Beginners — freeCodeCamp (YouTube):** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RGOj5yH7evk *(1 hr overview)*
- 🌐 **Learn Git Branching (interactive):** https://learngitbranching.js.org/

---

## 8. Summary (2 min)

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `git init` | Create a new repository |
| `git add` | Stage changes |
| `git commit` | Save a snapshot |
| `git branch` | List / create branches |
| `git checkout` | Switch branches or restore files |
| `git merge` | Combine branches |
| `git log` | View commit history |

---

## 9. References

1. Pro Git Book (free) — Scott Chacon & Ben Straub: https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2
2. Git Official Documentation: https://git-scm.com/docs
3. GitHub Git Guides: https://github.com/git-guides
4. Git and GitHub for Beginners — freeCodeCamp (YouTube): https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RGOj5yH7evk
5. Learn Git Branching (interactive): https://learngitbranching.js.org/

research_qc.summary: The lesson is factually accurate and strictly consistent with official Git reference documentation and the Pro Git book. Core command behavior (git init, add, commit, branch, merge) and repository state transitions are described accurately. Scope notice: This review checked claims against the curated source list; external live repositories were not polled.

findings.issue: The lesson introduces `git checkout` for switching branches; modern Git (2.23+) introduced `git switch` specifically to prevent confusing branch switching with file restoration.
The expected git log diagram uses placeholder hashes (`abc1234`). Learners should be reminded that SHA hashes are uniquely generated based on timestamp and author.

recommendations.text: Add a note highlighting modern Git 2.23+ `git switch` and `git restore` commands alongside `git checkout`.
recommendations.suggested_text: > 💡 **Modern Git Tip (Git 2.23+):** While `git checkout` is universal, newer Git versions introduce `git switch <branch>` (for switching branches) and `git restore <file>` (for un-staging changes) to make workflows clearer and safer.

recommendations.text: Add a note in the practical exercise reminding learners their commit SHA hashes will differ from the example.
recommendations.suggested_text: > 📌 *Note for learners: Your actual commit SHA hashes will differ from the example hashes (`abc1234`, `ghi9012`) because Git computes hashes using your exact commit timestamp and author details.*

instructional_qc.summary: The lesson provides an engaging, hands-on path toward the objective of tracking changes and branches. The 45-minute progression is realistic. A few additions around prerequisites and conflict practice will strengthen beginner self-study.

findings.issue: No installation instructions or system prerequisite verification before starting terminal commands.
Merge conflict markers are visually shown, but there is no hands-on micro-exercise for resolving a conflict step-by-step.
Knowledge check Q2 can be interpreted as either one command or two sequential commands.

recommendations.text: Add a prerequisites box instructing learners to install Git and configure their user identity before starting.
recommendations.suggested_text: > 📋 **Prerequisites:** Install Git from [git-scm.com/downloads](https://git-scm.com/downloads). Open your terminal and confirm with `git --version`, then set your name and email using `git config --global user.name "Your Name"` before beginning.

recommendations.text: Add a short hands-on mini-exercise for practicing merge conflict resolution.
recommendations.suggested_text:
### Optional Hands-on: Creating and Resolving Your First Merge Conflict
1. From `main`, create `branch-a`: edit line 1 of `README.md` to say `Version A`, then `git commit -am "Change on A"`.
2. Switch to `main`, create `branch-b`: edit line 1 of `README.md` to say `Version B`, then `git commit -am "Change on B"`.
3. On `branch-b`, run `git merge branch-a` — Git will announce a merge conflict in `README.md`.
4. Open `README.md`, remove `<<<<<<<`, `=======`, and `>>>>>>>`, keep the line you want, save, and run `git add README.md && git commit`.

recommendations.text: Clarify Knowledge Check Q2 to accept both single-command shortcuts and traditional two-command sequences.
recommendations.suggested_text: > 💡 *Tip for Q2:* Both the single-command shortcut (`git checkout -b <name>` or `git switch -c <name>`) and the two-command sequence (`git branch <name>` followed by `git checkout <name>`) are valid answers.
